subject: Human Body
title: Myelin and Signal Speed
description: A fast breakdown of Myelin and Signal Speed for builders.

hook.text: Some nerve signals travel at 270 mph. Others crawl at 2 mph. The difference is a fatty coating called myelin.

buildup.text: Myelin wraps around axons like insulation on a wire. Signals jump between gaps, skipping ahead at high speed.

discovery.text: This jumping pattern is called saltatory conduction. It's 100 times faster than unmyelinated nerve signals.

twist.text: Multiple sclerosis destroys myelin. Signals slow, scramble, or stop entirely.

climax.text: Babies myelinate gradually. That's why infants can't walk: motor nerves aren't insulated enough yet.

punchline.text: A thin layer of fat makes the difference between fast and slow.

quiz.question: What does myelin do for nerve signals?
options: Insulates axons so signals jump faster
